deep.reconstruction:
Context (previous page): Gauss has a lemma (the 'Hülfssatz'). For fixed k, consider the finite alternating series S = sum_{j=0}^k (-1)^j C(k,j) (1-theta)_j/(n+1)_j. Its sum is S = (n+theta)(n+theta+1)...(n+theta+k-1)/((n+1)(n+2)...(n+k)) = (n+theta)_k/(n+1)_k. In modern terms this is Chu–Vandermonde, 2F1(-k,1-theta;n+1;1) = (n+theta)_k/(n+1)_k. The lemma states that if S_m is the partial sum of the first m terms, then S - S_m has the sign of the first omitted term. On the previous page Gauss proved this for 1-theta>0, using the unimodality of the absolute values of the terms and working in from both ends.

This page:

(1) Proof strategy. Gauss remarks that the lemma is probably proved more easily by induction on k: from its validity up to some k, deduce it for k+1. He gives no details. A natural route (my suggestion, not on the page) is Pascal's rule C(k+1,j) = C(k,j) + C(k,j-1).

(2) Application. Gauss uses the lemma to bound the error of a transformed hypergeometric series. Let A = F(theta, n+theta, n+1, t^2), with Gauss's F(alpha,beta,gamma,x) = 2F1.
- Pfaff's transformation, F(a,b;c;x) = (1-x)^{-a} F(a, c-b; c; x/(x-1)), with c-b = n+1-(n+theta) = 1-theta, gives A = (1-t^2)^{-theta} F(theta, 1-theta, n+1, -t^2/(1-t^2)).
- B_mu is (1-t^2)^{-theta} times the sum of the first mu terms of that transformed series. The next omitted term is b_{mu+1}.
- First observation: (1-t^2)^{-theta-mu} has all Taylor coefficients of one sign (positive) once mu+theta>0.
- Claim: A - B_mu has the same sign as b_{mu+1}.

Implicit justification (mine). The j-th transformed term is (theta)_j (1-theta)_j/((n+1)_j j!) (-1)^j t^{2j} (1-t^2)^{-theta-j}. The coefficient of t^{2k} in t^{2j}(1-t^2)^{-theta-j} is (theta+j)_{k-j}/(k-j)!. So the t^{2k}-coefficient of the full transformed series is
(theta)_k/k! * sum_{j=0}^k (-1)^j C(k,j)(1-theta)_j/(n+1)_j = (theta)_k (n+theta)_k/(k!(n+1)_k),
which is the t^{2k}-coefficient of A. This is exactly where the Hülfssatz comes from.

Hence the t^{2k}-coefficient of A - B_mu equals (theta)_k/k! * (S^{(k)} - S^{(k)}_mu). By the lemma this has the sign of (theta)_k (-1)^mu (1-theta)_mu/(n+1)_mu. Since (theta)_k = (theta)_mu (theta+mu)...(theta+k-1) and theta+mu>0, every coefficient has the sign of (theta)_mu (1-theta)_mu (-1)^mu/(n+1)_mu, i.e. the sign of b_{mu+1} for 0<t^2<1. So the transformed series 'envelopes' A.

(3) Generalisation (statement begins here and continues on the next page). Gauss says the lemma is a special case of a more general one: if a, b, c, d, ... are positive and increasing, then any partial sum of a - k b + C(k,2) c - ... has the sign of the last term included. He proposes to apply it 'from the back'.
errors: No algebraic slip on this page; the Pfaff transformation and the setup of A, B_mu are correct.
The induction proof is only proposed, not carried out.
The tacit conditions are not stated: 0<t^2<1, n+theta>0 (or similar) so that the lemma applies for all k, and theta+mu>0.

The 'more general' lemma begun here and finished on the next page is false as stated, with mere positivity and monotonicity of a, b, c, ... . Counterexample: k=4, a=1, b=1.1, c=10, d=10.01 gives 1 - 4.4 + 60 - 40.04 = 16.56 > 0, although the last included term is negative. For full sums (m=k), k=2, a=1, b=2, c=2.5 gives -0.5 with the last term positive. Stronger hypotheses on the higher differences are needed (Abel summation gives sum_{j<=m} (-1)^j C(k,j) c_j = (-1)^m C(k-1,m) c_m - sum_{j<m} (-1)^j C(k-1,j) Delta c_j).

results.what: sum_j (-1)^j C(k,j)(1-theta)_j/(n+1)_j = (n+theta)_k/(n+1)_k, with partial sums enveloping it
results.modern_name: Chu–Vandermonde identity, plus a sign/enveloping property of its partial sums
results.usually_credited_to: Vandermonde (1772), Chu Shih-Chieh (1303) for the identity; the enveloping property is unclear

results.what: Truncation error of the Pfaff-transformed hypergeometric series has the sign of the first omitted term once theta+mu>0
results.modern_name: Enveloping series / error bounds for transformed hypergeometric series
results.usually_credited_to: Enveloping-series theory is usually associated with Stieltjes and Pólya–Szegő; specific bounds of this type appear later in the 19th–20th century

results.what: Proposed proof by induction on k

deep.surprise_reason: The Pfaff transformation and Chu–Vandermonde are known to have been used by Gauss (Disquisitiones circa seriem infinitam, 1812/13). The enveloping (error-sign) property of a transformed hypergeometric series, derived coefficientwise from a sign lemma on Vandermonde partial sums, is a nice unpublished detail of rigorous remainder estimation. It is not a major result attributed to someone else.
